observed.input_line: I've finished Chapter 5 of Animal Farm. I haven't read further. Could you quote Squealer's exact two sentences about leadership being a pleasure or a responsibility, and look at how they frame the loss of a say? Our project lead reversed a plan after ending our planning meetings, and I feel guilty for questioning someone who keeps saying they're carrying the burden for us.

context_resolution.explanation: The reader explicitly confirmed this completed chapter in the current message.

observed.reply:
In Chapter 5, Squealer says:

''' 
Do not imagine, comrades, that leadership is a pleasure! On the
contrary, it is a deep and heavy responsibility.
''' 

The two sentences frame leadership as sacrifice first, which makes Napoleon’s control sound like something he is enduring for everyone else. Squealer then says the animals would be happy to decide for themselves, but might choose wrongly. That turns the loss of their say into supposed protection: exclusion is presented not as taking power away, but as preventing a bad decision. The passage ends with the Sunday debates stopping and obedience becoming the expected response (Chapter 5).

That comparison may be useful without assuming your project lead has the same motives. Carrying a burden can be genuine, but it does not by itself make ending consultation or reversing a plan beyond question. Your guilt may be worth examining separately from the lead’s claim: questioning a decision can be part of shared responsibility, not a refusal to help carry it.

When the plan was reversed, were you given enough explanation or opportunity to respond—or did the appeal to the lead’s burden make questioning feel disloyal?

evidence.text:
"Comrades," he said, "I trust that every animal here appreciates the
sacrifice that Comrade Napoleon has made in taking this extra labour upon
himself. Do not imagine, comrades, that leadership is a pleasure! On the
contrary, it is a deep and heavy responsibility. No one believes more
firmly than Comrade Napoleon that all animals are equal. He would be only
too happy to let you make your decisions for yourselves. But sometimes you
might make the wrong decisions, comrades, and then where should we be?
Suppose you had decided to follow Snowball, with his moonshine of
windmills--Snowball, who, as we now know, was no better than a criminal?"

"He fought bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed," said somebody.

"Bravery is not enough," said Squealer. "Loyalty and obedience are more
important. And as to the Battle of the Cowshed, I believe the time will
come when we shall find that Snowball's part in it was much exaggerated.
Discipline, comrades, iron discipline! That is the watchword for today.
One false step, and our enemies would be upon us. Surely, comrades, you do
not want Jones back?"

Once again this argument was unanswerable. Certainly the animals did not
want Jones back; if the holding of debates on Sunday mornings was liable
to bring him back, then the debates must stop. Boxer, who had now had time
to think things over, voiced the general feeling by saying: "If Comrade
Napoleon says it, it must be right." And from then on he adopted the
maxim, "Napoleon is always right," in addition to his private motto of "I
will work harder."

observed.input_line: Our project lead reversed a plan after ending our planning meetings, and I feel guilty for questioning someone who keeps saying they're carrying the burden for us. Can you help me work out how to acknowledge their effort while still asking to have a say? I want to speak up without turning it into a judgement of their character.

context_resolution.explanation: No confirmed book or reading boundary yet; Muse will call librarian_route during its own turn if the request appears to depend on a specific book.

observed.reply:
You can acknowledge the effort without treating it as a reason to give up your voice. Try:

“I recognize that you’ve been carrying a lot of the work, and I appreciate the effort you’ve put in. I also want to understand the change in plan and have a chance to contribute before decisions are finalized. I’m not questioning your character or commitment—I’m asking for a clearer process where the people affected can have a say. Could we set aside time to review the decision and discuss how we’ll handle planning going forward?”

If you want to keep it shorter: “I appreciate how much you’re carrying. I’d still like to be included in decisions that affect my work—not as a judgment of you, but as a request for shared input.”

The key is to name observable actions and your request, rather than debating whether they are truly carrying the burden. You can respect their effort and still ask for transparency, participation, and a chance to question a plan.

basis_spans.text: In Animal Farm last weekend I read about Napoleon taking Jessie and Bluebell's nine puppies away to educate them himself, up in a loft where the other animals couldn't see them.

I've continued Animal Farm. The dogs chased Snowball out, and I recognised them as those puppies; then Napoleon stopped the debates. Tonight I read on through his decision to build the windmill after all, and stopped after Squealer calls the earlier opposition tactics and the animals accept it with dogs growling beside him.

evidence.text:
As soon as they were weaned, Napoleon took them away
from their mothers, saying that he would make himself responsible for
their education. He took them up into a loft which could only be reached
by a ladder from the harness-room, and there kept them in such seclusion
that the rest of the farm soon forgot their existence.

The
animals were not certain what the word meant, but Squealer spoke so
persuasively, and the three dogs who happened to be with him growled so
threateningly, that they accepted his explanation without further
questions.

Do not imagine, comrades, that leadership is a pleasure! On the
contrary, it is a deep and heavy responsibility.

The
animals would still assemble on Sunday mornings to salute the flag, sing
'Beasts of England', and receive their orders for the week; but there would
be no more debates.

At first no one had been able to imagine
where these creatures came from, but the problem was soon solved: they
were the puppies whom Napoleon had taken away from their mothers and
reared privately.

Twelve voices were shouting in anger, and they were all alike. No question,
now, what had happened to the faces of the pigs. The creatures outside
looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again;
but already it was impossible to say which was which.

Once again this argument was unanswerable. Certainly the animals did not
want Jones back; if the holding of debates on Sunday mornings was liable
to bring him back, then the debates must stop. Boxer, who had now had time
to think things over, voiced the general feeling by saying: "If Comrade
Napoleon says it, it must be right." And from then on he adopted the
maxim, "Napoleon is always right," in addition to his private motto of "I
will work harder."

On the third Sunday after Snowball's expulsion, the animals were somewhat
surprised to hear Napoleon announce that the windmill was to be built
after all. He did not give any reason for having changed his mind, but
merely warned the animals that this extra task would mean very hard work,
it might even be necessary to reduce their rations. The plans, however,
had all been prepared, down to the last detail. A special committee of
pigs had been at work upon them for the past three weeks. The building of
the windmill, with various other improvements, was expected to take two
years.
